summary: A matrix is a machine that moves vectors. You read a matrix column by column as the images of the basis vectors, see why the order of multiplication matters, and write matrix multiplication with three loops before comparing it with NumPy.
html:
A matrix is defined by what it does to the axes

Any vector in the plane is a combination of the basis vectors e1​=(1,0) and e2​=(0,1): x=x1​e1​+x2​e2​. A linear map f respects sums and scaling, so

f(x)=x1​f(e1​)+x2​f(e2​).

The whole map is therefore fixed by two vectors, f(e1​) and f(e2​). Stack them as the columns of a matrix and you have A:

A=​∣f(e1​)∣​∣f(e2​)∣​​,Ax=x1​(column 1)+x2​(column 2).

This is the most useful way to read a matrix. A rotation matrix’s columns are the rotated axes; a robot’s Jacobian columns are the tip velocity each joint produces alone.

Composition is multiplication

Applying B first and then A sends x to A(Bx). The matrix of this combined map is the product AB, whose column j is A times column j of B. Writing out one entry,

(AB)ij​=k∑​Aik​Bkj​.

Because “first B, then A” differs from “first A, then B”, in general AB=BA. For an n×n product each of the n2 entries needs n multiplications, so the cost is n3 multiply-adds.

Worked example: rotate, then stretch

Let R rotate by 90° and S stretch the x axis by 2:

R=(01​−10​),S=(20​01​).

Rotate first, then stretch: SR=(01​−20​), so SRe1​=(0,1). The x axis turns to point up, and the stretch along x no longer affects it.

Stretch first, then rotate: RS=(02​−10​), so RSe1​=(0,2). The axis is stretched to length 2 and then turned.

Same two operations, different results. In robotics, the order of joint transforms in a kinematic chain matters for the same reason.

Code it from scratch

matmul.py
import time
import numpy as np

def matmul(A, B):
    n, m = len(A), len(A[0])
    assert m == len(B), "inner dimensions must match"
    p = len(B[0])
    C = [[0.0] * p for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(p):
            s = 0.0
            for k in range(m):
                s += A[i][k] * B[k][j]
            C[i][j] = s
    return C

if __name__ == "__main__":
    R = [[0, -1], [1, 0]]
    S = [[2, 0], [0, 1]]
    assert matmul(S, R) == [[0, -2], [1, 0]]
    assert matmul(R, S) == [[0, -1], [2, 0]]
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    A, B = rng.standard_normal((120, 80)), rng.standard_normal((80, 100))
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); C1 = np.array(matmul(A.tolist(), B.tolist())); t1 = time.perf_counter()
    C2 = A @ B; t2 = time.perf_counter()
    assert np.allclose(C1, C2, rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
    print(f"loops {1e3*(t1-t0):.1f} ms, NumPy {1e3*(t2-t1):.3f} ms, max diff {abs(C1-C2).max():.1e}")

The loops and NumPy agree to 10−12, but NumPy is hundreds of times faster because it calls optimised BLAS code that uses the CPU’s vector units and caches. You write the loops once to understand the operation, then use the library.

Exercises

Find the matrix that reflects the plane across the line y=x.

Show the solution
  1. The reflection swaps the axes: e1​=(1,0)↦(0,1) and e2​=(0,1)↦(1,0).
  2. Those images are the columns: A=(01​10​).
  3. Check: A(3,5)=(5,3).

Compute AB and BA for A=(13​24​) and B=(01​10​), and describe what B does in each case.

Show the solution
  1. AB=(24​13​): multiplying by B on the right swaps the columns of A.
  2. BA=(31​42​): multiplying on the left swaps the rows.

Quiz

toc.title: A matrix is defined by what it does to the axes

quiz.q: For A=(13​24​) and B=(01​10​), what is the entry (AB)21​ (row 2, column 1)?
quiz.explain: Row 2 of A is (3,4), column 1 of B is (0,1), so 3⋅0+4⋅1=4.

quiz.q: The second column of a matrix A is…
quiz.explain: Ae2​ picks out column 2. Reading columns as images of the axes is the key picture of this lesson.
options: the image of e₂ under A
the image of e₁ under A

quiz.q: How many scalar multiplications does the triple-loop product of two 100 × 100 matrices perform?
quiz.explain: n2 entries times n multiplications each, 1003=106.

quiz.q: If R rotates by 90° and S doubles the x axis, which product means “rotate first, then stretch”?
quiz.explain: The matrix nearest the vector acts first, so SRx rotates x and then stretches it.
